lessons.title: How a verse is built
lessons.summary: Phrases, marks and the two halves of a verse
lessons.goal: After this you can hear that a verse is made of short phrases, each with its own small tune.
body: Torah is chanted, not read. Every word carries a small mark, above or below a letter, and the marks tell the reader which tune to sing. You do not need to read music. You need to hear about ten short tunes and know which mark each one belongs to.
The marks come in phrases. A phrase is two or three words that run together and end on a mark with a tune of its own. The colour on this site belongs to the whole phrase, not to one word.
Every verse has two halves. The first half rests on a mark called etnachta. The second half ends on sof pasuk. Listen for the rest, then the ending.
lessons.listenFor: Two places where the tune settles: a rest in the middle of the verse, and a lower, final landing at the end.

examples.why: Two phrases: the rest on etnachta, then the ending.

Short, clear, and the rest comes early.

lessons.title: Sof pasuk
lessons.summary: Where the verse ends
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the end of a verse coming and know the mark that ends it.
body: Sof pasuk is the ending. It is the only phrase that is in every single verse, so it is the first tune to learn. The last word carries a small vertical line under its stressed syllable, and the verse closes with a colon-like sign.

The phrase is usually three words: mercha, tipcha, then the ending. Mercha stays level. Tipcha lifts and falls back. The last word steps down to the lowest note of the verse and stays there. Sometimes a fourth word, a second mercha, comes between tipcha and the end.
When you hear the tune land low and stop, the verse is over. Breathe there.
lessons.listenFor: The last word drops to the lowest note in the verse and rests on it.

examples.why: Three words that end the verse: mercha, tipcha, sof pasuk. The last line of the priestly blessing.
Four words: mercha, tipcha, mercha, then the end.
The second half of the Shema, four words.
Two words: tipcha straight into the end, no mercha.
Two words again, in a verse you may know as a song.
The ending on a single word, with nothing before it.

lessons.title: Etnachta
lessons.summary: Where the verse rests
lessons.goal: After this you can hear where a verse rests in the middle, and tell that rest from the ending.
body: Etnachta is the rest in the middle of the verse. Its mark looks like a small wishbone under the stressed syllable. Nearly every verse has one, and it splits the verse into two halves of meaning.

The phrase is usually tipcha, munach, etnachta, or just tipcha and etnachta. Tipcha lifts and falls, as it did before the ending. Munach steps down. Then etnachta climbs back up and holds a note in the middle of the range, where the tune rests but does not finish.
Sof pasuk lands low and closes. Etnachta stays up and waits. That difference is the first thing to listen for.
lessons.listenFor: Before the rest the tune steps down, then rises and holds a middle note, waiting rather than closing.

examples.why: The first three words of the Torah: tipcha, munach, etnachta.
Two words, tipcha straight into etnachta. The Shema.

lessons.title: Zakef
lessons.summary: The most common phrase inside a verse
lessons.goal: After this you can hear zakef, the most common phrase inside a verse, and the marks that lead into it.
body: Zakef katan is two dots above the stressed syllable, one over the other. It is the commonest pause inside a verse: a small comma, not a rest.

Its tune is a peak: up to a high note, then down to settle. The words before it set it up. Pashta sits high and holds, on a mark at the very end of the word. Mahpach, a small angle, swings low first. Munach steps gently. A full phrase runs mahpach, pashta, munach, zakef; two words, munach and zakef, are very common.
Sometimes a whole zakef phrase sits on one word, with munach and zakef both on it. Yetiv, a mark before the first letter, opens a zakef phrase too.
lessons.listenFor: A climb to a high note, then a drop that settles without closing; pashta before it sits high and still.

examples.why: Two words: munach, zakef. The simplest form.

lessons.title: Revia
lessons.summary: A slow walk down
lessons.goal: After this you can hear revia's slow walk down and tell it from zakef's peak.
body: Revia is a single dot above the word, like a small diamond. It marks a pause a little weaker than zakef, often on the first word of a verse or right before a new thought.
The tune walks down: four steps, one after another, landing well below where it started. Nothing leaps. If a munach comes before it, the munach rises first, so the phrase goes up, then slowly down.
Zakef peaks and drops; revia only descends. Munach followed by a short vertical bar, called legarmeh, takes the same place as revia and sings a small tune of its own; the site colours it as revia.
lessons.listenFor: Four even steps downward, like coming down a short staircase, with no leap.

lessons.title: Tevir
lessons.summary: A dip, often after darga
lessons.goal: After this you can hear tevir's dip and the darga that often leads into it.
body: Tevir is a dot with a small tail, under the stressed syllable. It is a short pause, and it often comes a word or two before an etnachta or a sof pasuk.

The tune dips: down a step, down again, then back up to settle. The word before it is often darga, a zigzag under the word, which comes down the scale to meet tevir. Or it is a mercha that lifts and drops onto tevir. Kadma can come before either.
Etnachta rises to a rest; tevir dips and recovers, and the verse keeps going.
lessons.listenFor: A dip below the line and a climb back, in one word; darga before it winds down to meet it.

examples.why: Darga, tevir on the first two words.

lessons.title: Kadma v'azla
lessons.summary: A climb, with geresh and gershayim
lessons.goal: After this you can hear kadma v'azla's climb and know its two cousins, geresh and gershayim.
body: Kadma v'azla is a pair: kadma, a small hook above the word, then azla, a single slanted stroke above the next. Together they lead into a longer phrase, often one that ends on revia or zakef.
The tune climbs. Kadma starts low. Azla goes up, wobbles at the top, and holds. It sounds like a question being set up.

The same slanted stroke on its own is called geresh, and a double stroke is gershayim. They sing close relatives of the azla tune, and this site colours all three the same. Kadma looks like pashta but sits on the stressed syllable, not at the end of the word.
lessons.listenFor: A climb that reaches high, wavers once at the top, and holds there.

lessons.title: Segol
lessons.summary: The long zarka and the short segol
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the long winding zarka and the short segol that answers it.
body: Segol is three dots above the end of a word, the shape of the segol vowel turned over. It comes with zarka, a curved stroke above the end of the word before it. The pair comes less often than the phrases you already know, and it usually sits near the start of a long verse.
Zarka is the longest tune so far: it winds down and down, step by step. Segol then answers with a short turn and settles.
A munach often opens the phrase. A very rare mark, shalshelet, a zigzag above the word, is a long chain of the same tune; it appears only four times in the Torah, and this site colours it with segol.
lessons.listenFor: A long winding descent on zarka, then a short turn that settles on segol.

lessons.title: Telisha ketana
lessons.summary: A small turn into the next phrase
lessons.goal: After this you can hear telisha ketana's small turn and know it leads into the phrase after it.
body: Telisha ketana is a small circle with a tail, above the end of the word. It has one of the smallest tunes in the system: a quick turn, down a step and back, that settles on the note it came from.
It is a joining mark, not a pause, and it almost always leads into kadma v'azla or into a longer phrase. This site gives it its own colour because it is easy to hear once you know it.
Its bigger cousin, telisha gedola, sits at the start of the word and sings a long climb; it lives in the pazer lesson.
lessons.listenFor: A quick small turn on one word, down and back, that leads straight into the next phrase.

lessons.title: Pazer
lessons.summary: A tall arch, and telisha gedola
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the tall arch of pazer and the long climb of telisha gedola.
body: Pazer is a small branching mark above the word. It is a minor pause early in a long verse, and it has one of the highest tunes in the system: a climb to the sixth note, then a tumble back down.

Telisha gedola, a circle with a tail at the start of the word, is grouped with it here. Its tune climbs to the fifth and walks back down to where it began. The two are easy to tell apart by shape: pazer goes higher and falls faster.
Karnei farah, a double-horned mark that appears once in the Torah, is grouped here too. A munach often comes first.
lessons.listenFor: A tall climb and a fall back down on one word; telisha gedola climbs and walks back more evenly.

lessons.title: Zakef gadol
lessons.summary: The larger zakef, on a word of its own
lessons.goal: After this you can hear zakef gadol and tell it from the small zakef you already know.
body: Zakef gadol is zakef's bigger form: the two dots with a vertical line beside them. It stands on its own word with no words leading in, which is why it needs a bigger tune to fill the space.
The tune rises, holds high with a small lean, and comes back down to settle. Zakef katan is a quick peak; zakef gadol stays up longer and ends the same way. If you hear the peak hold, it is gadol.
This is the last of the Torah families. After it you can hear everything in a regular verse.
lessons.listenFor: A rise that holds at the top with a small lean, then settles; longer than the small zakef's peak.

lessons.title: Your first verse
lessons.summary: Lein the Torah's first verse, Genesis 1:1
lessons.goal: After this you have leined Genesis 1:1, one part at a time and then whole.
body: You can hear all ten phrases. Now put them together on one verse: Genesis 1:1, the first verse of the Torah. It has two parts, and you have learned every mark in it.

Learn it one part at a time. Hear the first part, chant it back, then try it without the recording. Do the same with the second part, then connect the two and chant the whole verse. Breathe at the rest and at the end.
The reader's version is one good version. If your cantor or tutor sings a phrase differently, theirs wins. For another verse after this one, try Exodus 25:8. It is shorter.
lessons.listenFor: Your own voice landing the rest and the ending where the reader does.

examples.why: The starter verse: two phrases, a rest and the ending.
The prepared alternative: shorter, two phrases, a rest and the ending.

lessons.title: Sof pasuk in the haftarah
lessons.summary: The ending, in the haftarah tune
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah ending, which settles on the home note instead of dropping below it.
body: The haftarah uses the same marks and the same phrases as the Torah, with a different set of tunes. The mode is minor.

The ending is the first difference to hear. In the Torah the last word drops to the lowest note. In the haftarah, tipcha falls low first; then the last word rises to the third and falls back onto the home note, the note the whole tune keeps returning to.
The words are the same: mercha, tipcha, sof pasuk.
lessons.listenFor: Tipcha falls low, then the last word rises and falls back onto the home note.

examples.why: Tipcha, sof pasuk: two words, in the haftarah of comfort.

lessons.title: Etnachta in the haftarah
lessons.summary: The rest, in the haftarah tune
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah rest, which rocks before it settles.
body: The rest in the middle of the verse is longer in the haftarah than in the Torah. Tipcha rises a little and holds. Munach steps down. Then etnachta rocks between the home note and the third, rises to the fifth, and settles on the fourth.
So the rest does not finish the thought: it leaves the tune hanging above home, and the second half of the verse brings it down.
The marks are unchanged: tipcha, munach, etnachta.
lessons.listenFor: A rocking figure between home and the third, a rise, and a settle on the fourth, hanging rather than closing.

lessons.title: Zakef in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A short step up and a drop
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah zakef, a short step up and a drop.
body: Zakef in the haftarah is shorter than in the Torah: one step up, then a drop of two. Pashta before it sits high and falls one step, and mahpach swings down to the home note first.
The munach that comes right before zakef has a tune of its own here, with a leap up near its end. Listen for that leap: it tells you a zakef is coming.
Yetiv, before the first letter, opens the phrase with a high note that falls.
lessons.listenFor: A small step up and a two-step drop; the munach before it leaps upward as a warning.

lessons.title: Revia in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A walk down to home
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah revia, which walks down to home and touches it twice.
body: Revia walks down here too, but it goes all the way to the home note, bounces up to the third, and lands on home again. It is longer than the Torah revia and ends more firmly.
The munach before it leaps up to the top note and comes straight back. When you hear that leap, a revia follows.
lessons.listenFor: A walk down to the home note, a touch above, and home again; the munach before it leaps up high.

lessons.title: Tevir in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A drop to the bottom and a climb back
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah tevir, a drop to the bottom and a climb back.
body: Tevir in the haftarah drops to the home note, dips once below it, and climbs back to the third. It is deeper than the Torah tevir.
Darga before it starts high and walks down four steps to meet it. Mercha before it leaps up and comes back.
lessons.listenFor: A drop to the bottom, a dip below it, and a climb back; darga before it walks down from high.

lessons.title: Kadma v'azla in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A leap to the top of the range
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah azla, with its leap to the top of the range.
body: Kadma v'azla in the haftarah starts with a plain kadma, then azla climbs, leaps up to the octave, and drops back. It is the widest phrase in the haftarah tune.
Geresh on its own winds up and down more gently. Gershayim rises and holds high. All three share a colour here, as in the Torah.
lessons.listenFor: A climb, a leap to the very top, and a drop back; gershayim rises and holds instead.

lessons.title: Segol in the haftarah
lessons.summary: Zarka and segol, in the haftarah tune
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah zarka and segol.
body: Zarka winds down here as it does in the Torah, from the fifth note all the way to the home note and a touch below. Segol answers with a rise to the fifth and a step down.
The pair is less common in the haftarah than in the Torah, so it stands out when it comes.
lessons.listenFor: A winding descent to the bottom, then a short rise and a step down.

lessons.title: Telisha ketana in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A longer turn than the Torah's
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah telisha ketana, which is longer than the Torah's.
body: In the Torah, telisha ketana has one of the smallest tunes there is. In the haftarah it grows: it holds on the fourth note, turns up to the fifth, and walks down to home. It still leads straight into the phrase after it.
lessons.listenFor: A held note, a turn upward, and a walk down to home, all on one word that leads on.

lessons.title: Pazer in the haftarah
lessons.summary: A climb to the octave
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah pazer, which climbs to the octave.
body: Pazer climbs here too, as high as the haftarah tune goes: up to the octave and back down in one long sweep. Telisha gedola climbs only to the fourth and walks back, so it is the quieter of the two, as in the Torah.
lessons.listenFor: A long sweep up to the octave and all the way back; telisha gedola is the same shape at half the height.

lessons.title: Zakef gadol in the haftarah
lessons.summary: The larger zakef, in the haftarah tune
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the haftarah zakef gadol.
body: Zakef gadol stands alone on its word here too. The tune leaps to the fifth, falls to the home note, and settles on the third: a wide swing down, where the small zakef is a short step.
lessons.listenFor: A leap up, a fall to the bottom, and a settle on the third; wider than the small zakef.

lessons.title: The end of the haftarah
lessons.summary: The ending of the whole haftarah
lessons.goal: After this you can hear the special ending that closes the whole haftarah.
body: The last verse of a haftarah ends with its own tune. The marks are the ordinary ones, mercha, tipcha, sof pasuk, but the melody is bigger. Tipcha walks down from high. Then the last word rises to the octave and settles on the sixth, held long, so the room knows the reading is over.
This is an ending context, not a separate mark. The site colours the last phrase of a haftarah in its own colour so you can see it coming.
This is the last of the families. After it you can hear everything in a haftarah.
lessons.listenFor: On the last word of the haftarah, a rise to the top and a long held settle, instead of the usual quiet close.

notes.families: Family ids and names follow src/lib/trope/chart-catalog.ts. confusedWith drives distractor weighting (ACTIVITIES.md, item generation rules).
notes.items: Each activity's items is the planned count; a lesson's drills may stop early once eight items in a row have been answered right with no miss, and missed items are re-asked until each is right once.
notes.lookAlikes: Look-alike pairs (ACTIVITIES.md #9). Each word's ref, word number (a maqaf-joined pair is one word), text and mark were checked against the engine on 2026-10-23; azla is the stroke after a kadma, geresh the same stroke with none before it. azla-geresh is reading only (Daniel, 2026-10-23).
notes.practice: Practice runs that are not lessons. Quick ten opens once its melody's third family is heard and answers the name cards, as hear-and-name does.
